evidence: This is an inference from the structural observations.

claim: Small spines with fewer AMPA receptors may be more susceptible to disappear after several hours of sleep because they lack the strong cytoskeleton network that usually anchor the receptors to the membrane.
source: Small spines with fewer AMPA receptors may be more susceptible to disappear after several hours of sleep because they lack the strong cytoskeleton network that usually anchor the receptors to the membrane.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on molecular knowledge.

claim: Branched synapses may be especially vulnerable because their average strength, as measured by the size of the ASI, is even smaller than that of non-branched synapses.
source: Branched synapses may be especially vulnerable because we found that their average strength, as measured by the size of the ASI, is even smaller than that of non-branched synapses.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's data.

claim: The removal of branched synapses during sleep may trigger the disappearance of the postsynaptic density (PSD) followed by the detachment of the presynapse, hence the disappearance of the synapse and, in some cases, even of the spine housing that synapse.
source: In turn, the removal of branched synapses during sleep may trigger the disappearance of the postsynaptic density (PSD) followed by the detachment of the presynapse, hence the disappearance of the synapse and, in some cases, even of the spine housing that synapse.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic interpretation of the findings.

claim: This hypothesis could be tested directly in vivo using two-photon repeated imaging to track the same cerebellar synapses across the sleep/wake cycle.
source: This hypothesis could be tested directly in vivo using two-photon repeated imaging to track the same cerebellar synapses across the sleep/wake cycle, as we recently did for cortical synapses (Miyamoto et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experiments based on previous work.

claim: The glutamatergic synapses of the cerebellum follow rules of plasticity that partly diverge from those prevalent in the forebrain.
source: It should also be mentioned that the glutamatergic synapses of the cerebellum follow rules of plasticity that partly diverge from those prevalent in the forebrain.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on cerebellar plasticity.

claim: The long-term potentiation of the parallel fiber synapses was required for vestibulo-cerebellar motor learning and relied on AMPA receptors containing the GluR3 subunit.
source: A recent study Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017 found that the long-term potentiation of the parallel fiber synapses was required for vestibulo-cerebellar motor learning and relied on AMPA receptors containing the GluR3 subunit, rather than the GluR1 subunit commonly involved in cortical and hippocampal plasticity (Diering and Huganir, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on cerebellar plasticity.

claim: GluR3-mediated synaptic potentiation did not involve the trafficking of the receptors but resulted from an increase in open channel probability.
source: GluR3-mediated synaptic potentiation did not involve the trafficking of the receptors but resulted from an increase in open channel probability (Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on cerebellar plasticity.

claim: At least some forms of synaptic potentiation in the parallel fiber synapses do not rely on the insertion of AMPA receptors in the synaptic membrane and are not expected to increase the size of the synapses and the size of the ASI.
source: Thus, at least some forms of synaptic potentiation in the parallel fiber synapses do not rely on the insertion of AMPA receptors in the synaptic membrane and are not expected to increase the size of the synapses and the size of the ASI.
evidence: This is an inference from cited studies on cerebellar plasticity.

claim: The endocytosis of GluR2-containing AMPA receptors is key for the long-term depression of the parallel fiber synapses.
source: On the other hand, the endocytosis of GluR2-containing AMPA receptors is key for the long-term depression of the parallel fiber synapses (Chung et al., 2003; Steinberg et al., 2006) as it is the case for many cortical and hippocampal synapses (Diering and Huganir, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on synaptic plasticity.

claim: In the adult cerebellum the glutamate receptor delta 2 is specifically expressed in the parallel fiber synapses and has been involved in long-term depression and in the maintenance of these synapses.
source: Of note, in the adult cerebellum the glutamate receptor delta 2 is specifically expressed in the parallel fiber synapses and has been involved in long-term depression and in the maintenance of these synapses (Mandolesi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on cerebellar receptors.

claim: In a genome-wide transcriptomic analysis of cerebellar transcripts affected by sleep and wake, the mRNA coding for the delta 2 subunit was upregulated after sleep.
source: In a genome-wide transcriptomic analysis of cerebellar transcripts affected by sleep and wake, we found that the mRNA coding for the delta 2 subunit was upregulated after sleep (Cirelli et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a cited transcriptomic study.

claim: Whether changes in the expression of the delta 2 receptor contribute to the synaptic changes described here is not known and could be explored in future studies.
source: Whether changes in the expression of this receptor contribute to the synaptic changes described here is not known and could be explored in future studies.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: The cerebellar cortex is involved in the early phases of cerebellar learning, while later stages involve the cerebellar and vestibular nuclei downstream.
source: Several studies have shown that the cerebellar cortex is involved in the early phases of cerebellar learning, while later stages involve the cerebellar and vestibular nuclei downstream (D'Angelo et al., 2016; Canto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on cerebellar learning.

claim: The study could only examine structural changes in synapses across sleep and wake in a restricted portion of cerebellar cortex that contains a relatively homogeneous population of Purkinje cells.
source: Because of the labor-intensive nature of ultrastructural studies, we could only examine structural changes in synapses across sleep and wake in a restricted portion of cerebellar cortex that contains a relatively homogeneous population of Purkinje cells.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the study.

claim: In the vermal lobule VI, most or all Purkinje cells express the molecular marker zebrin II.
source: In the area that we targeted, the vermal lobule VI, most or all Purkinje cells express the molecular marker zebrin II (Cerminara et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited anatomical studies.

claim: Zebrin positive and zebrin negative Purkinje cells differ in many structural and functional parameters.
source: Zebrin positive and zebrin negative Purkinje cells differ in many structural and functional parameters, from the dominant type of climbing fiber input that they receive to the level of intrinsic excitability and spiking activity (Zhou et al., 2014; Cerminara et al., 2015; Viet et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Purkinje cell heterogeneity.

claim: The extent to which the current results extend to zebrin negative Purkinje cells is unknown.
source: The extent to which the current results extend to zebrin negative Purkinje cells is unknown.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the study.

claim: Zebrin negative cells express stronger intrinsic and synaptic plasticity relative to zebrin positive cells.
source: On the other hand, zebrin negative cells express stronger intrinsic and synaptic plasticity relative to zebrin positive cells (Wadiche and Jahr, 2005; Viet et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Purkinje cell heterogeneity.

claim: In the cerebral cortex, sleep/wake changes in ASI size are accompanied by several changes in the peripheral astrocytic processes surrounding many cortical synapses.
source: In the cerebral cortex, we previously reported that the sleep/wake changes in ASI size are accompanied by several changes in the peripheral astrocytic processes surrounding many cortical synapses.
evidence: This is supported by cited previous studies.

claim: Astrocytic processes contain more numerous but smaller glycogen granules after spontaneous and forced wake compared to sleep, suggesting increased glycogen turnover to meet the high energy demand of wake.
source: Specifically, these processes contain more numerous but smaller glycogen granules after spontaneous and forced wake compared to sleep, suggesting increased glycogen turnover to meet the high energy demand of wake (Bellesi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a cited ultrastructural study.

claim: After a few hours of sleep deprivation astrocytic processes get closer to the synaptic cleft, likely reflecting an increased need for glutamate clearance.
source: Moreover, after a few hours of sleep deprivation astrocytic processes get closer to the synaptic cleft, likely reflecting an increased need for glutamate clearance (Bellesi et al., 2015), and astrocytic phagocytosis of synaptic elements is increased (Bellesi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited ultrastructural studies.

claim: Astrocytic phagocytosis of synaptic elements is increased after sleep deprivation.
source: Moreover, after a few hours of sleep deprivation astrocytic processes get closer to the synaptic cleft, likely reflecting an increased need for glutamate clearance (Bellesi et al., 2015), and astrocytic phagocytosis of synaptic elements is increased (Bellesi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a cited ultrastructural study.

claim: Bergmann glia establish extensive contacts with parallel fiber synapses.
source: Bergmann glia, the astrocytic cells of the cerebellum, establish extensive contacts with parallel fiber synapses and their distal processes respond to the electrical stimulation of the parallel fibers with localized increases in calcium levels (Grosche et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Bergmann glia.

claim: The distal processes of Bergmann glia respond to the electrical stimulation of the parallel fibers with localized increases in calcium levels.
source: Bergmann glia, the astrocytic cells of the cerebellum, establish extensive contacts with parallel fiber synapses and their distal processes respond to the electrical stimulation of the parallel fibers with localized increases in calcium levels (Grosche et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Bergmann glia.

claim: Calcium signaling in Bergmann glia can modulate the activity of neighboring Purkinje cells.
source: Calcium signaling in Bergmann glia can, in turn, modulate the activity of neighboring Purkinje cells (Wang et al., 2012), in line with strong neuron-glia crosstalk.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on neuron-glia interactions.

claim: Bergmann glia express AMPA receptors, which are required for the normal development of the parallel fiber synapses.
source: Moreover, contrary to cortical astrocytes, Bergmann glia express AMPA receptors, which are required for the normal development of the parallel fiber synapses (Saab et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Bergmann glia.

claim: Bergmann glia is routinely involved in the phagocytosis of synaptic and extrasynaptic elements, a process that increases after motor learning.
source: Bergmann glia is also routinely involved in the phagocytosis of synaptic and extrasynaptic elements, a process that increases after motor learning (Morizawa et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Bergmann glia.

claim: Future experiments should test whether sleep and wake affect the structure and function of Bergmann glia.
source: Thus, given the multiple ways Bergmann glia can modulate cerebellar activity (De Zeeuw and Hoogland, 2015), and specifically the parallel fiber synapses that are the focus of the current study, future experiments should test whether sleep and wake affect the structure and function of these cells.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: Very little is known about the effects of sleep and wake on cerebellar physiology.
source: Very little is known about the effects of sleep and wake on cerebellar physiology (Canto et al., 2017), and the available evidence is mostly confined to the Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is supported by a cited review.

claim: The simple spike activity of Purkinje cells is lower during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep than during wake or REM sleep.
source: Both their simple spike activity, which is driven by the excitatory inputs from parallel fiber synapses, and their complex spike activity, which reflects the excitatory input from a single climbing fiber, are lower during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep than during wake or REM sleep (Mano, 1970; Marchesi and Strata, 1971; Hobson and McCarley, 1972; Harlay et al., 1974; Canto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited electrophysiological studies.

claim: The complex spike activity of Purkinje cells is lower during NREM sleep than during wake or REM sleep.
source: Both their simple spike activity, which is driven by the excitatory inputs from parallel fiber synapses, and their complex spike activity, which reflects the excitatory input from a single climbing fiber, are lower during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep than during wake or REM sleep (Mano, 1970; Marchesi and Strata, 1971; Hobson and McCarley, 1972; Harlay et al., 1974; Canto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited electrophysiological studies.

claim: The response of Purkinje cells to microiontophoretically applied glutamate is smaller in NREM sleep than in wake.
source: The response of Purkinje cells to microiontophoretically applied glutamate is also smaller in NREM sleep than in wake (Andre and Arrighi, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a cited electrophysiological study.

claim: The decreased response of Purkinje cells to glutamate in NREM sleep is not accounted for by changes in spontaneous firing rate but may be associated with the decreased level of acetylcholine and noradrenaline in NREM sleep.
source: This effect is not accounted for by changes in spontaneous firing rate but may be associated with the decreased level of acetylcholine and noradrenaline in NREM sleep, which is observed across the brain, including in the cerebellum (Andre and Arrighi, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a cited electrophysiological study.

claim: Whether the sleep-wake cycle is accompanied by changes in the number or strength of synaptic connections in the cerebellum was completely unknown prior to this study.
source: However, whether the sleep-wake cycle is also accompanied by changes in the number or strength of synaptic connections was completely unknown.
evidence: This establishes the knowledge gap addressed by the study.

claim: The cerebellum shows ultrastructural synaptic changes consistent with an overall upregulation during wake and down-selection during sleep.
source: As shown here through serial electron microscopy, the cerebellum, like the cerebral cortex and the hippocampus, also shows ultrastructural synaptic changes consistent with an overall upregulation during wake and down-selection during sleep (Tononi and Cirelli, 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings in the context of cited theoretical frameworks.

claim: The selective changes in branched synapses across wake and sleep suggest that, during wake, coincidences of firing over parallel fibers may translate into the formation of synapses coincident over the same branched spine.
source: The selective changes in branched synapses across wake and sleep also suggest that, during wake, coincidences of firing over parallel fibers may translate into the formation of synapses coincident over the same branched spine, which may be especially effective at driving the soma of Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: During sleep, off-line activity over parallel fibers may lead to the pruning of branched synapses that were formed due to spurious coincidences.
source: During sleep, off-line activity over parallel fibers may instead lead to the pruning of branched synapses that were formed due to spurious coincidences (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: This interpretation is consistent with electrophysiological, anatomical, and modeling studies showing that many parallel fiber synapses are silent.
source: While speculative, this interpretation is consistent with electrophysiological, anatomical, and modeling studies showing that (1) many parallel fiber synapses are silent and (2) given the exorbitant number of these synapses, information storage is promoted when only some of them are effective (eloquent).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Given the exorbitant number of parallel fiber synapses, information storage is promoted when only some of them are effective (eloquent).
source: While speculative, this interpretation is consistent with electrophysiological, anatomical, and modeling studies showing that (1) many parallel fiber synapses are silent and (2) given the exorbitant number of these synapses, information storage is promoted when only some of them are effective (eloquent).
evidence: This is supported by cited modeling studies.
